items.followUp: Describe the role of chlorophyll and water in the light reactions of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Light absorption initiates the light reactions.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
rubric.how: Award for stating that chlorophyll absorbs light energy.

rubric.why: Water splitting supplies electrons and releases oxygen.
rubric.description: Water is split by photolysis, releasing oxygen, protons and electrons.
rubric.how: Award for identifying photolysis and at least one of its products.

rubric.why: Electron transfer through carriers is a key event in the light reactions.
rubric.description: Light-excited electrons pass through electron carriers.
rubric.how: Award for describing the transfer of excited electrons through carriers.

rubric.why: The light reactions produce ATP.
rubric.description: Energy from electron transfer is used to form ATP from ADP and phosphate.
rubric.how: Award for stating that ATP is formed.

rubric.why: Reduced NADP is another product used in the next stage of photosynthesis.
rubric.description: NADP is reduced to NADPH; oxygen is released as a by-product.
rubric.how: Award for identifying NADPH formation or the release of oxygen as a product of the light reactions.

modelAnswer: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, exciting its electrons.
The excited electrons pass through a series of electron carriers.
Water molecules split by photolysis to replace the lost electrons, releasing protons and oxygen.
Energy released during electron transfer is used to form ATP from ADP and phosphate; this is photophosphorylation.
NADP accepts electrons and protons to form NADPH; oxygen is released as a by-product.

items.followUp: Name five mineral nutrients required by plants and state one role of each.

rubric.why: The answer must give roles for two nutrients to establish breadth.
rubric.description: Gives roles for nitrogen and phosphorus.
rubric.how: Award for linking nitrogen to protein or chlorophyll formation and phosphorus to energy transfer or ATP formation.

rubric.why: Potassium is an essential nutrient with roles in enzyme activity and stomatal function.
rubric.description: Gives a role of potassium.
rubric.how: Award for linking potassium to enzyme activity or stomatal function.

rubric.why: Magnesium is a component of chlorophyll.
rubric.description: Gives the role of magnesium.
rubric.how: Award for stating that magnesium is part of the chlorophyll molecule.

rubric.why: Calcium contributes to the structure of plant cells.
rubric.description: Gives a role of calcium.
rubric.how: Award for linking calcium to cell-wall or cell-membrane structure.

modelAnswer: Nitrogen is needed to make amino acids and proteins; it is also a component of chlorophyll.
Phosphorus is needed to make ATP and nucleic acids and is important in energy transfer.
Potassium helps activate enzymes and regulates the opening and closing of stomata.
Magnesium is a constituent of chlorophyll and is therefore essential for photosynthesis.
Calcium is needed for the formation and stability of cell walls and cell membranes.

items.followUp: Explain how humidity, wind and temperature affect the rate of transpiration.

rubric.why: Temperature changes the rate of evaporation from leaf surfaces.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of temperature.
rubric.how: Award for stating that higher temperature generally increases transpiration by increasing evaporation.

rubric.why: Humidity affects the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and air.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of humidity.
rubric.how: Award for stating that low humidity or dry air increases transpiration.

rubric.why: Moving air removes the moist air layer around leaves.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of wind.
rubric.how: Award for stating that wind increases transpiration by removing water vapour around the leaf.

rubric.why: Light commonly affects stomatal opening and thus water loss.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of light.
rubric.how: Award for stating that light generally opens stomata and increases transpiration, while darkness tends to reduce it.

rubric.why: Water availability affects whether stomata remain open and water can be supplied to leaves.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of water availability in the soil.
rubric.how: Award for stating that adequate soil water supports transpiration, while water shortage may cause stomata to close and reduce it.

modelAnswer: High temperature increases evaporation of water from leaf surfaces and generally increases transpiration.
Low humidity (dry air) increases the difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and the air, increasing transpiration.
Wind removes the moist air around the leaf, maintaining the water-vapour gradient and increasing transpiration.
Light generally causes stomata to open, increasing transpiration; darkness usually reduces it as stomata close.
Adequate soil water allows continued water loss, whereas a shortage of soil water may cause stomata to close and reduce transpiration.

items.followUp: Write the scientific names of wheat and the housefly.

rubric.why: This identifies mustard by its scientific name.
rubric.description: Gives the scientific name of mustard.
rubric.how: Award for the accepted scientific name of mustard.

rubric.why: This identifies frog by its scientific name as given in the textbook or accepted current taxonomy.
rubric.description: Gives the scientific name of frog.
rubric.how: Award for the accepted scientific name of frog.

modelAnswer: Mustard: Brassica campestris.
Frog: Rana tigrina.

items.followUp: What is a host organism? Give one example of a parasite and its host.

rubric.why: A parasite lives on or in another organism.
rubric.description: Defines a parasite as living on or in a host.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a parasite lives on or in a host organism.

rubric.why: A parasite obtains nourishment from its host, generally harming it.
rubric.description: Explains how a parasite benefits at the host's expense.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it obtains food or nourishment from the host, or harms the host.

modelAnswer: A parasite is an organism that lives on or inside another organism, called its host.
It obtains food or nourishment from the host and usually harms it.

items.followUp: State two observations that supported the idea that mosquitoes spread malaria.

rubric.why: The first observation links the occurrence of malaria with the presence or breeding places of mosquitoes.
rubric.description: Gives one observation connecting malaria with mosquitoes or mosquito-prone places.
rubric.how: Award for stating that malaria was commonly observed where mosquitoes were abundant or near stagnant water.

rubric.why: A second relevant observation links seasonal mosquito abundance or protection from mosquitoes with malaria occurrence.
rubric.description: Gives a second observation supporting a connection between mosquitoes and malaria.
rubric.how: Award for stating that malaria and mosquitoes were both common in warm or rainy seasons, or that people protected from mosquito bites were less likely to get malaria.

modelAnswer: A.F.A. King observed that malaria was common in places where mosquitoes were abundant, particularly near stagnant water.
He also noted that malaria and mosquitoes were common during the same warm or rainy seasons.

items.followUp: Give two differences between a plant primary cell wall and a secondary cell wall.

rubric.why: Thickness is a key structural difference between the two walls.
rubric.description: States that the primary cell wall is thin and gives a contrasting feature of the secondary wall.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the primary wall as thin and the secondary wall as thicker.

rubric.why: The walls differ in when they form and whether they can expand.
rubric.description: States when the walls form or whether the primary wall can expand.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the primary wall forms during cell growth and is extensible, while the secondary wall forms after growth has stopped.

modelAnswer: The primary cell wall is thin and flexible, whereas the secondary cell wall is thicker and often strengthened with lignin.
The primary wall forms while the cell is growing and can expand; the secondary wall is deposited inside the primary wall after growth has stopped.

items.followUp: Why are viruses considered non-living outside a host but living inside a host?

rubric.why: Viruses show a life-like ability to reproduce only inside host cells.
rubric.description: States a living characteristic of viruses inside a host.
rubric.how: Award for stating that viruses reproduce or multiply inside living host cells.

rubric.why: Outside a host, viruses lack independent cellular activity and can show non-living properties.
rubric.description: States a non-living characteristic of viruses outside a host.
rubric.how: Award for stating that viruses are inactive or lack metabolism outside a host, or that they can be crystallized.

modelAnswer: Inside a living host cell, a virus reproduces by using the cell's machinery, showing a living characteristic.
Outside a host, it has no independent metabolism or cellular activity and can be crystallized, showing non-living characteristics.
Therefore, viruses are considered to lie at the borderline between living and non-living organisms.
